article.title: COP31 went up in flames over fossil fuels — it sends an important message
article.summary:
Anyone hoping for bold action on climate change has many reasons to be disappointed by the latest United Nations climate summit, COP31, which concluded in a dramatic overtime session on 22 November.
After gathering for nearly two weeks in the beach resort city of Antalya, Turkey, in what will probably be the hottest year on record, representatives from nearly all the world’s countries failed to agree on a plan to tackle climate change.
Almost 100 nations walked out without signing a ‘cover decision’ — a non-binding statement meant to push for ambitious action — because the document did not call on the world to transition away from fossil fuels.
The last COP climate talk to break down this badly was the Copenhagen summit in 2009.
But when language targeting fossil fuels disappeared from the draft cover decision after lobbying by oil-rich nations, a coalition of around 90 countries, led by the European Union and small island states, rejected the agreement.

article.summary:

The growth is likely driven by refugee and displaced students from Nepal, Colombia and Iran, all countries that have recently been devastated by natural disasters or political upheaval.
The report doesn’t include students with temporary protected status; those designated as refugees, asylum seekers or humanitarian parolees; or other displaced students already living in the U.S.

article.title: How Realistic Are Foreign-Policy Realists?
article.summary:
Foreign-policy realists are the killjoys of international politics.
They have no choice but to pursue their interests—though realists disagree among themselves about what those are.
“Defensive” realists think states desire security above all.
“Offensive” realists think states are driven to maximize power.
But all realists agree that the laws of power cannot be avoided any more than the law of gravity.
